text: Two cousins leave a refugee camp at Peshawar and set out for London, overland, the way people travel when the other ways are closed. Jamal is the younger of them; the plan is a chain of arrangements — a snowbound pass into Turkey crossed on foot, then west by whatever will carry them, then Paris, then a claim for asylum at the far end. Michael Winterbottom treats the route itself as the story, and the tension is simply whether each handover holds. Eighty-eight minutes is short for a journey of that length, which forces the film into ellipsis: distance passes in the cuts, and the waiting gets the screen time. European juries gave it best film, best director and, tellingly, best cinematography — a prize for images gathered on the move rather than composed at rest.

The money changes hands first, and what it buys is only company. Armando is fifty, lives in Caracas, and approaches young men in the street with an offer that stops well short of what either party assumes it means. Elder is seventeen and runs a gang, so setting terms is his trade; these terms are not his. Lorenzo Vigas lets the imbalance stand instead of resolving it — age against youth, money against need, a city that has already sorted the two of them into positions — and ninety-three minutes is exactly long enough for the question of who is using whom to lose its outline. Venice gave it the Golden Lion and Venezuela sent it on to the Academy. Neither of them has language for what he wants, and the film does not supply any.

Two people in this household have come back from Algiers, and neither brings the past home in a form that can be said out loud. Hélène sells antique furniture in Boulogne and lives with her stepson Bernard, lately out of the army. Her old lover Alphonse arrives with his niece Françoise, having run a café over there himself. Bernard talks about a fiancée, Muriel, whom Hélène has never met. What follows is meals, errands and an attempted renewal between two middle-aged people, conducted by everyone at a slight angle to everyone else — an answer a beat late, a memory that does not fit the room it is told in. Venice's prize for best actress belongs to the performance at the centre of that, a part whose work is done in tone rather than in anything it says.

An errand sets it going: a farmer in Inner Mongolia rides to the nearest town for contraceptives, because policy has fixed how many children he may have. On the way back he hauls a Russian truck driver out of a lake and takes him home. Nikita Mikhalkov plays much of that for comedy — the visitor appalled by the household, then charmed by it, then unwilling to leave — and the household absorbs him the way it absorbs weather. Two hours, a French production spoken in Russian, set among people who are neither. The prizes arrived from every direction at once: Golden Lion, César, European Film Award for best film, the Academy's international category. What the farm may not survive is not the guest himself but what a guest implies.

Madrid, 1942, and the war is over: the men who won it are making money quickly, and the poets are counting coins in cafés. Mario Camus adapts Camilo Jose Cela's novel by keeping its method rather than straightening it out — dozens of lives, sampled instead of followed, a city assembled out of overheard conversation. Nobody is granted a full arc; the film moves between tables the way the book moves between paragraphs, and hunger is the one thing continuous across all of them. It is a comedy in the sense that people are funny when performing a dignity they cannot afford, and the joke has a bill attached. Berlin's Golden Bear went to it, forty years after the year it reconstructs, from a distance that let that year be looked at plainly.

A hairdresser's apprentice needs a Porsche by the day of his first race and has no honest way of getting one. Eighty-five minutes suits that exactly: the film runs on the logic of acquisition, each bad idea recruiting a worse one, everyone he meets assessed for whether they bring the car nearer. A girl turns up in the middle of it and is filed, for a while, under the same heading. Jerzy Skolimowski shot it in Belgium in French in 1967 and pitched it at the speed of someone who has not yet learned that wanting a thing is different from being owed it. Berlin's Golden Bear landed on this, a serious prize for a comedy about a boy and a car. What he stands to lose while chasing it is arranged in the background, where he never looks.

The telling is left entirely to bodies: three unrelated stories, ninety-three minutes, danced rather than spoken. Gene Kelly directed, and the constraint has consequences all the way down — plot has to arrive as gesture, motive as rhythm, a joke assembled out of timing with no line to land it. The genre listing pairs music with fantasy, which is the plain description of what happens to a room once it is no longer obliged to behave. Ninety-three minutes is a long stretch to sustain with nothing spoken to lean on, and that risk is the interesting part: it holds second by second or it does not hold. A Golden Bear came back from Berlin, a European jury answering an American picture that had removed the one element needing translation.

The day-care centre in this film is a boat, moored on the Seine in the middle of Paris. Adults living with mental illness come aboard by day; the structure gives them a place to be and a time to be there, which turns out to be most of what the word care means in practice. Nicolas Philibert spends 109 minutes inside it, alongside a staff trying to hold the thing open against a psychiatry that keeps getting thinner. What that yields is a documentary made of ordinary transactions — a conversation, a task, a routine repeated — filmed at the pace they actually take. Berlin's Golden Bear went to it and European juries named it best documentary. A building that floats is a strange argument for stability, and it is the argument being made.

Seven episodes, roughly fifteen minutes each, and ten commandments to get through. The arithmetic is the joke: Julien Duvivier's 1963 portmanteau doubles some sins up and skips past others, and the register shifts without warning — a servant who cannot stop blaspheming in one, a novice walking out of his order over a family injury in the next, a man buying jewellery for a woman who already bores him. Two hours, French, and a Golden Bear on its record, which is a lot of institutional respect for a film organised around bad behaviour. Fifteen minutes is not long in which to damn anybody, so the time goes on making each sin look reasonable first, right up to the point where it stops being funny.

Georges Bizet's opera, sung in Xhosa, in the township the title names. The score stays; nearly everything usually attached to it goes — the Seville of the 1875 libretto, the proscenium, the assumption that this music arrives with a certain kind of audience. What crosses over intact is the centre of the thing: a woman who insists on choosing, in a place organised around men who expect to do the choosing, and the pull between people who damage each other and keep coming back. Mark Dornford-May filmed it on location, in the language spoken there, which gives a repertory standard an actual address. Berlin's Golden Bear followed in 2005. Two hours of Bizet in Xhosa, and the melodies take it without complaint.

Sören Mårtensson teaches middle school, and the room of half-grown children in front of him is taking something out of him that does not come back. Jan Troell gives this 110 minutes, a long stretch for a man who is not in crisis so much as in slow erosion: lessons going nowhere, a class that has taken his measure, the daily arithmetic of being outnumbered. Sweden, 1968, and Berlin's Golden Bear landed on a film whose largest event is a working week and whose antagonist is a timetable. Teaching here is labour, not vocation. The nights belong to the job as well — he is haunted in sleep by the work — which is the quietest way of saying it has stopped being something he can leave at the door.

A famous writer from the capital drives out to the provinces in search of a subject, which is already the wrong way round. Kim Yesenin has the reputation, the phrases and the practised melancholy; what he meets are people whose difficulties refuse to arrange themselves into material — Sasha, and Andrei, a dissident preparing to leave for America. That this was made in the Soviet Union in 1979, with that word and that plan on screen, is worth registering before anything else about it. The Golden Bear and the critics' FIPRESCI prize at Berlin both went to it. Gleb Panfilov keeps to ninety-eight minutes, most of them talk, and lets the pressure fall on one man's discovery that his sadness has been a career rather than a condition.
